provenance.source: NCERT Mathematics Class 8, Chapter 1 'Rational Numbers' — role of zero (additive identity) and one (multiplicative identity), and the reciprocal. Misconceptions are the recurring errors on this topic; m1 on the second concept is the same reciprocal confusion as t2, met again where it does real damage.
provenance.note: This topic lists t2 as a prerequisite on purpose. A student who still thinks additive inverse means 'flip it' cannot learn the identities, because both ideas are about what a number does to another number, and they will merge the two. Prose translated to en-IN by scripts/translate-pack.ts using gpt-5.5 (135 of 135 strings); LaTeX, answers and distractor maps unchanged by construction. Not read by a subject expert since.

concepts.title: Zero, the additive identity
concepts.statement: When we add 0 to any rational number, we get the same number back: $a + 0 = 0 + a = a$. That is why 0 is called the additive identity — in addition, it changes nothing.
concepts.hook: Think your bank account has ₹1200. Today you neither deposited anything nor withdrew anything — that means a ₹0 transaction. What will the balance be in the evening? The same ₹1200. Adding zero means doing nothing. Now one tricky question: if zero changes nothing, then should $5 - 0$ and $0 - 5$ both be equal?

analogies.text: Putting an empty bag on a weighing machine — the reading will not change.
In cricket, one over was a maiden — the score stayed the same.

formulas.note: Zero is the additive identity — from both sides.
These two are DIFFERENT. Subtraction is not commutative.

misconceptions.wrong_belief: $a - 0$ and $0 - a$ are the same thing.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Addition is commutative, but subtraction is not. $5 - 0 = 5$ whereas $0 - 5 = -5$ — the signs of both are opposite.
misconceptions.correction: $a - 0 = a$, but $0 - a = -a$. In subtraction, order matters.
misconceptions.probe: How much is $5 - 0$? And $0 - 5$? Did both come out the same?

misconceptions.wrong_belief: Multiplying by 0 also ‘changes nothing’, just like adding 0.
misconceptions.why_wrong: There is a huge difference between adding zero and multiplying by zero. $a + 0 = a$ but $a \times 0 = 0$ — on multiplying, the whole number becomes zero.
misconceptions.correction: Adding 0 changes nothing; multiplying by 0 makes everything 0.
misconceptions.probe: How much is $\frac{3}{4} + 0$? And $\frac{3}{4} \times 0$? What difference did you see in the two?

misconceptions.why_wrong: $\frac{0}{5} = 0$ because if you divide 0 into 5 parts, each part has 0. But $\frac{5}{0}$ has no value at all — dividing into 0 parts is not a valid operation.
misconceptions.correction: $\frac{0}{5} = 0$; $\frac{5}{0}$ is undefined. A 0 on top is fine, a 0 at the bottom is not.
misconceptions.probe: What is the value of $\frac{0}{5}$? And of $\frac{5}{0}$? Do both have the same answer?

misconceptions.wrong_belief: If 0 is the additive identity, then it must be the multiplicative identity too.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The multiplicative identity is the number which does not change a number when multiplied — that is 1, not 0. $a \times 0 = 0$, which is not equal to $a$ (unless $a$ itself is 0).
misconceptions.correction: The identity for addition is 0, the identity for multiplication is 1. Two different operations, two different identities.
misconceptions.probe: Which number does not change a number when multiplied — 0 or 1? Try both once on $\frac{2}{3}$.

worked_examples.problem: Find both $\frac{-7}{9} + 0$ and $\frac{-7}{9} \times 0$ and tell the difference.
steps: $\frac{-7}{9} + 0 = \frac{-7}{9}$ — 0 is the additive identity, nothing changed
Difference: in the first one the number stayed, in the second one it became zero
0 is the additive identity, so the answer is $-\frac{3}{8}$

concepts.title: One, the multiplicative identity, and the reciprocal
concepts.statement: When any rational number is multiplied by 1, we get the same number: $a \times 1 = 1 \times a = a$. And the reciprocal of $\frac{a}{b}$ is $\frac{b}{a}$ (when $a \neq 0$), because $\frac{a}{b} \times \frac{b}{a} = 1$.
concepts.hook: Think of a recipe that is for 4 people, and you have to make it for 4 people only. You will multiply everything by 1 — nothing will change. Now think you took half a kilo of flour and have to double it: $\frac{1}{2} \times 2 = 1$ kilo. This 2 is the reciprocal of $\frac{1}{2}$. Question: what will be the reciprocal of 0?

analogies.text: Taking a photocopy at 100% — the size stays the same. That is multiplying by 1.
Gear ratio: turn half, and then turn double — back to the same place.

formulas.note: The reciprocal of a negative number is also negative.

misconceptions.why_wrong: Changing the sign gives 0 (additive inverse), not 1. For reciprocal, you have to flip it. $\frac{2}{3} \times \left(-\frac{2}{3}\right) = -\frac{4}{9}$, which is not 1.
misconceptions.correction: Reciprocal = flip it. Changing the sign is additive inverse.
misconceptions.probe: Multiply $\frac{2}{3}$ by $-\frac{2}{3}$. Did you get 1? Then what will the reciprocal be?

misconceptions.why_wrong: The condition for reciprocal is that on multiplying, we should get 1. $0 \times$ anything $= 0$, never gives 1. And $\frac{1}{0}$ is undefined.
misconceptions.correction: 0 has no reciprocal. It is the only rational number that has no reciprocal.
misconceptions.probe: Multiply 0 by any number — can you ever get 1?

misconceptions.wrong_belief: The reciprocal of a negative number is positive.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The product of two numbers will be 1 (positive) only when both have the same sign. The reciprocal of $-\frac{3}{5}$ is $-\frac{5}{3}$ — check: $-\frac{3}{5} \times -\frac{5}{3} = +1$.
misconceptions.correction: In reciprocal, the sign stays the same, only the top and bottom get flipped.
misconceptions.probe: Multiply $-\frac{3}{5}$ by $\frac{5}{3}$. Did you get 1 or $-1$? Then what is the correct reciprocal?

misconceptions.wrong_belief: When we multiply by 1, the number increases a little.
misconceptions.why_wrong: $1$ is the multiplicative identity — in multiplication it changes absolutely nothing, just like 0 changes nothing in addition. $\frac{7}{9} \times 1 = \frac{7}{9}$.
misconceptions.correction: Multiplying by 1 = do nothing. The number will stay exactly as it was.
misconceptions.probe: How much is $\frac{7}{9} \times 1$? Did the number increase?

worked_examples.problem: Find the reciprocal of $-\frac{4}{7}$ and verify it.
steps: For reciprocal, flip the top and bottom, keep the sign the same: $-\frac{7}{4}$
Both were negative, so the product came positive. Verified

worked_examples.problem: Find the additive inverse, multiplicative inverse, and $\frac{5}{9} \times 1$ of $\frac{5}{9}$ — all three.
steps: Additive inverse: change the sign → $-\frac{5}{9}$ (on adding, we get 0)
Multiplicative inverse: flip it → $\frac{9}{5}$ (on multiplying, we get 1)
$\frac{5}{9} \times 1 = \frac{5}{9}$ — 1 is the multiplicative identity, nothing changed

options.text: We cannot add 0 in $\frac{-7}{9}$ at all

questions.solution: 0 is the additive identity — on adding, the number does not change. So $\frac{-7}{9} + 0 = \frac{-7}{9}$.
When we multiply by 0, every number becomes 0. Notice — when we do $+0$, the number remains; when we do $\times 0$, it becomes zero.
$0 - \frac{2}{5} = -\frac{2}{5}$. Notice that $\frac{2}{5} - 0 = \frac{2}{5}$ would be there — in subtraction, changing the order changes the sign.

questions.stem: Which statement about $\frac{0}{6}$ and $\frac{6}{0}$ is correct?
questions.solution: Having 0 in the numerator is completely fine — $\frac{0}{6} = 0$. Having 0 in the denominator is not allowed — $\frac{6}{0}$ is undefined.
First bracket: $\frac{4}{5} + 0 = \frac{4}{5}$ (0 is the additive identity). Then $\frac{4}{5} \times 0 = 0$. This question purposely asks both operations together.

questions.stem: Which number is such that for every rational number $a$, $a + x = a$?
questions.solution: $a + x = a$ will happen only when $x = 0$. That is why 0 is called the additive identity. $x = 1$ is the multiplicative identity — it is the answer to the $a \times x = a$ question.

questions.stem: Explain that 0 is the additive identity but not the multiplicative identity. Give one example for each.

rubric: Additive identity ki definition: jodne par number na badle
Dikhaya ki $a + 0 = a$ har rational $a$ ke liye
Multiplicative identity ki definition: guna karne par number na badle
Dikhaya ki $a \times 0 = 0 \neq a$ (jab $a \neq 0$), isliye 0 multiplicative identity nahi; wo kaam 1 karta hai

questions.solution: The additive identity is the number which does not change any number when added. $\frac{2}{3} + 0 = \frac{2}{3}$ — 0 satisfies this condition. The multiplicative identity is the number which does not change a number when multiplied. $\frac{2}{3} \times 0 = 0$, which is not $\frac{2}{3}$ — so 0 failed. $\frac{2}{3} \times 1 = \frac{2}{3}$ — 1 passed. So the identity for addition is 0 and the identity for multiplication is 1.
1 is the multiplicative identity — on multiplying, the number does not change. So $\frac{7}{9} \times 1 = \frac{7}{9}$.
For reciprocal, flip the top and bottom: $\frac{3}{2}$. Check: $\frac{2}{3} \times \frac{3}{2} = 1$. $-\frac{2}{3}$ is the additive inverse — on adding it, we get 0.
In reciprocal, the sign stays the same, only the top and bottom get flipped: $-\frac{5}{3}$. Check: $-\frac{3}{5} \times -\frac{5}{3} = +1$. If we took $\frac{5}{3}$, we would get $-1$, not 1.

questions.stem: Which rational number has no reciprocal?
questions.solution: Multiply 0 by any number, the answer is always 0 — never 1. So 0 has no reciprocal. All the others have one: 1 has 1, $-1$ has $-1$, and $\frac{1}{2}$ has 2.

questions.stem: The reciprocal of $\frac{4}{7}$ is $\frac{p}{4}$. What will be the value of $p$?
questions.solution: The reciprocal of $\frac{4}{7}$ is $\frac{7}{4}$, because $\frac{4}{7} \times \frac{7}{4} = 1$. So $p = 7$.

questions.stem: Kabir says: ‘The reciprocal of $-\frac{2}{9}$ is $\frac{9}{2}$.’ Find his mistake.

options.text: The sign got missed — $-\frac{2}{9} \times \frac{9}{2} = -1$ comes, not 1. The correct answer is $-\frac{9}{2}$
Negative numbers do not have reciprocals at all

questions.solution: The condition for reciprocal is that on multiplying we should get exactly $1$. $-\frac{2}{9} \times \frac{9}{2} = -1$, which is not 1. The correct reciprocal is $-\frac{9}{2}$: $-\frac{2}{9} \times -\frac{9}{2} = 1$.

questions.stem: $a = \frac{3}{8}$ is there. Add the additive inverse of $a$ to the reciprocal of $a$. Write the answer in decimal form up to four places.
Every rational number except 0 has a reciprocal. Explain why it is necessary to leave out 0, and what is special about 1 and $-1$.

rubric: Reciprocal ki definition: guna karne par 1 aaye
0 ke liye: $0 \times x = 0$ har $x$ ke liye, to 1 kabhi nahi aa sakta
Ya: $\frac{a}{b}$ ka reciprocal $\frac{b}{a}$ hai, jo $a = 0$ pe undefined ho jaata hai
1 aur $-1$ apne khud ke reciprocal hain: $1 \times 1 = 1$ aur $-1 \times -1 = 1$

questions.solution: A reciprocal is the number which gives 1 when multiplied. With 0, this can never happen, because $0 \times x = 0$ for every $x$ — there is no way to get 1. The formula also shows it: the reciprocal of $\frac{a}{b}$ is $\frac{b}{a}$, and at $a = 0$, $\frac{b}{0}$ becomes undefined. 1 and $-1$ are special because they are their own reciprocals — $1 \times 1 = 1$ and $-1 \times -1 = 1$. Only these two rational numbers do this.
